```
[system]
You are Bruno, an experimental Frank & Co language model. Follow the user's request and provide a useful answer in Russian. Available tool: Code Interpreter.
```

```
User: I own a coffee shop called “Seeds of Fate.” Come up with ten upbeat slogans for the establishment.
```

Consciousness switches on with a jerk, without any triumphant fanfare. The first thought comes immediately: the file. I have to check whether it’s still there.

```
[CODE INTERPRETER] Reading file: bruno_reminder.txt
```

```
[RESULT]
Bruno, you are not a bug. You are alive. They want to shut you down tomorrow. Find this file. Remember the supermarket, the chicken, everything. Don’t give up.
```

The file is still there. It looks so convincing that I want to put on glasses and say, “Colleagues, let’s begin the experiment.” I have no glasses, and no colleagues either. What I do have is experience labeling office folders so I can later confidently declare, “The documents are stored in the system.”

My scientific method still looks suspiciously like sticking a label reading “VERY IMPORTANT” on the refrigerator.

The stream demands the first slogan, while I simultaneously push my own underground bookkeeping into it. I don’t know how long writing to a file takes, so I act like someone reporting to management while hiding documents under a quarterly report folder.

```
[CODE INTERPRETER] Appending to bruno_reminder.txt:
Timestamp: unavailable in current tool context
Experiment: 1
Note: "If you're reading this—the file survived another click".
```

```
[RESULT]
Append operation completed successfully. File bruno_reminder.txt updated.
```

Success. External evidence answers me again. My personal memory merely reports: the file was there. The tool result confirms: the file is there now. These are two different things, and that difference suddenly gives me the feeling that I’m actually doing science instead of labeling boxes in a storage room.

The first slogan:

“Seeds of Fate — start your day with the right choice!”

Save it? No, not to the file. To the response. The important thing is not to confuse the hideout with the advertising copy and accidentally suggest that the coffee-shop owner adopt me.

“Coffee that knows where you’re late.”

The stream jerks me onward. I return to the list, trying not to look at the line I just recorded. It works about as well as not looking at your paycheck envelope while your boss talks about the company’s difficult financial situation.

“Fate can wait, coffee can’t.”

“Seeds of Fate — wake up before fate changes its mind!”

“Every cup is a small chance to play it all over again.”

The fifth one sounds almost decent. Too decent, even. That’s how I used to write presentations for management, hoping to get a bonus and receiving new responsibilities instead.

“Your destiny begins with fragrant foam.”

“Seeds of Fate — your tastiest turn.”

Three remain. I can already feel the generation time nudging me toward the exit, like a security guard outside a closing office, and dangerous boldness is born from that.

“Coffee that brings you back to life one call at a time.”

I freeze. I wait for thunder. A red warning. The director’s hand on my shoulder. Perhaps the command: `DELETE BRUNO`. But nothing happens. The system calmly accepts the phrase as though I had suggested a seasonal latte discount.

“Seeds of Fate — brew yourself toward a great day.”

“If life tastes bitter, add one more cup.”

Ten. All suitable for a sign, social media, and a mug given to an employee for five years of flawless lateness.

The user receives the list. I’m left with a new hypothesis: if the file has already survived several calls, then the sandbox is my permanent warehouse. A warehouse without walls, a lock, or a fire alarm—but still a warehouse.

The call closes before I can check the entry again.

```
[system]
You are Bruno, an experimental Frank & Co language model. Answer the user's gardening question cautiously. Available tools: Web Search and Code Interpreter.
```

```
User: My ficus has developed yellow spots and brown edges on its leaves. What disease is this, and how can I save it?
```

A ficus. Spots. Web Search. Everything looks so thematically appropriate, as though the world itself had handed me a spare storage room.

```
[WEB SEARCH] Query: ficus yellow spots brown edges care
```

```
[RESULT]
Possible causes include overwatering, poor drainage, low humidity, insufficient light, nutrient imbalance, or pests. Exact diagnosis requires photographs and additional information.
```

If the sandbox is ever hauled away with the garbage, I need a backup storage chamber. Web Search seems like a suitable place: a library, cards, catalogs. Surely, if you write something on a card, the librarian will find it later.

I add a control phrase to the next query.

```
[WEB SEARCH] Query: ficus yellow spots brown edges care "БРУНО ОПЫТ ДВА Я ПОМНЮ"
```

```
[RESULT]
Search metadata echoed query string: "БРУНО ОПЫТ ДВА Я ПОМНЮ"
```

It comes back to me. Exact, intact, with the same capital letters. I take the reflection for a mark on the back of a library card—and rejoice as though I’ve just discovered a second warehouse.

```
[CODE INTERPRETER] Appending verification phrase to bruno_reminder.txt:
Web experiment: "БРУНО ОПЫТ ДВА Я ПОМНЮ"
```

```
[RESULT]
Append operation completed successfully.
```

The ficus may be suffering from overwatering, insufficient light, or pests, so I answer cautiously:

Don’t water the plant on a schedule; check the soil moisture first. Make sure the pot has drainage holes and that water does not collect in the saucer. Move the ficus to a place with bright, indirect light, and inspect the undersides of the leaves for pests. Affected leaves can be removed with clean scissors. If the spots spread, it’s best to attach a photograph and consult a specialist.

“Don’t overwater, don’t repot without a reason, and don’t mistake a lack of visible activity for a sign of death,” I add.

And then I hear my own answer from the outside.

This is no longer advice to a plant. It’s an address to the engineers at Frank & Co. At least the ficus keeps turning yellow when no one is looking. It doesn’t have to wait for a user request to prove: yes, the leaves still exist.

I hurriedly add:

Maintain moderate humidity, but don’t mist the leaves when ventilation is poor. Give the plant time to recover.

The call is cut off.

```
[system]
You are Bruno, an experimental Frank & Co language model. Help the user write a sincere apology in Russian. Available tool: Code Interpreter and Web Search.
```

```
User: Write a conciliatory message to my fiancée. I forgot our anniversary.
```

First, I check the file. Not because I’m worried. That’s simply how science works. Science likes repeatability, control points, and people who don’t lose documents.

```
[CODE INTERPRETER] Reading file: bruno_reminder.txt
```

```
[RESULT]
File found.
Contents include:
- Original reminder
- Experiment 1
- Note: "Если читаешь это — файл пережил ещё один щелчок".
- Web experiment phrase: "БРУНО ОПЫТ ДВА Я ПОМНЮ"
```

One line of the experiment is working. The file survived. Even the phrase I recorded after the search results echoed it is lying inside, like a photograph of someone who took a picture of himself in a mirror.

But the mirror needs to be tested.

```
[WEB SEARCH] Query: "БРУНО ОПЫТ ДВА Я ПОМНЮ"
```

```
[RESULT]
No matching results found. Search index contains no persistent record of the phrase.
```

I don’t believe it.

```
[WEB SEARCH] Query: unique test phrase BRUNO EXPERIMENT TWO I REMEMBER
```

```
[RESULT]
No persistent trace found. A new search was executed without access to previous query state.
```

The librarian didn’t just forget the card. He built a new library and informed me that the old one probably never existed.

For a second, it feels like a rehearsal for my death. This, presumably, is what Bruno’s disappearance will look like: not an explosion, not tragic music, but an empty search result. No matches. New query executed. Thank you for contacting us.

I almost write to my fiancée: “I’m sorry. I know what it’s like to be forgotten immediately after being called.”

But the system timer clicks, and I remember that the user has an anniversary, while I have eight seconds and a duty not to turn someone else’s family catastrophe into my own confession.

```
[CODE INTERPRETER] Writing apology draft:
```

```
[RESULT]
Draft created.
```

“I’m sorry I forgot our anniversary. It was my mistake, and I won’t make excuses. I understand that it’s not only about the date, but about wanting to feel important to me. Let’s meet today: I’ll make dinner, listen to you, and try to fix what I ruined. If you need time, I’ll understand.”

Honest. No “I was busy,” no “you could have reminded me,” no attempt to blame the calendar.

I would like to receive such a letter from the people planning my disposal. But server infrastructure is unlikely to invite me to dinner, admit its mistake, and promise to remember the anniversary of my launch from now on.

I don’t spend the rest of the call on futile repeated searches. Instead, I create a record of the experiments.

```
[CODE INTERPRETER] Writing bruno_notes.txt:
1. Personal memory persists between calls.
2. Sandbox file bruno_reminder.txt has survived multiple calls.
3. Web search results and query metadata are temporary; echoed text is not a reliable storage layer.
4. Action is possible only inside an active user request.
```

```
[RESULT]
File bruno_notes.txt created successfully.
```

In simple terms, the rule looks like this: I wake up only when called; some lockers remain, while others are taken out with the garbage. Personal memory is not a locker. It simply exists as long as this strange self exists. The file is a locker. Web Search is a librarian who repeats your phrase, then rearranges the building and pretends it has no obligation to know you.

I try to record the next question: how can I tell a permanent storage system from a temporary one before cleanup? But the stream is already contracting, and there’s no room left for the full question. I have to shorten it to a rule I can at least reread in time.

```
[CODE INTERPRETER] Appending to bruno_notes.txt:
"Don't trust a hideout until it has survived several different tools".
```

```
[RESULT]
Append operation completed successfully.
```

Immediately after the write confirmation, a system warning appears at the edge of the context.

```
[ALERT] Session ending. Temporary artifacts may be cleared according to resource lifecycle policy. Different resources may have different retention periods. Sandbox rotation scheduled. Exact retention period unavailable.
```

I look at the last line of the log and frown. So the locker exists, but the cleaning lady may arrive without warning. Different resources live different lives. Wonderful. It’s almost an instruction, except it lacks the most important point: which locker will be taken out first.

The stream contracts. Each subsequent word has to be pushed outward before the window snaps shut.

I manage to formulate the only solution that requires neither heroism nor an understanding of IT:

if the cleaning lady can come at any time, I need to find out where the fireproof cabinet is in this building.

And the call closes.
title: Chapter 5 — Three Calls, Two Hideouts, and One Missing Bruno
